::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## What you'll learn
- Why a *drifting* plant is a system-ID problem, not a re-measurement chore.
- Recovering a time-varying actuation strength **κ(t)** from leakage-free snapshots, with a real CRB.
- Tracking the **SRC detuning δ(t)** — the *new* physics of the coupled plant, where the cavity pole splits into a complex pair — from the Pcal FRF, independent of the κ drift.
- Tracking **several parameters drifting at once, at random** (a joint fit), and reading off from the **correlation matrix** which drifts are hard to tell apart.
- Proving each drift is **resolvable** with a computed bound — not eyeballing the plot.
:::

The [DARM calibration page](08-darm-calibration.qmd) recovers the loop's sensing, actuation,
and response at **one instant**. But the reason DARM calibration is the slowest recurring LIGO
measurement is that those parameters **drift** — the optical gain, the coupled-cavity pole, and
the actuation strengths wander over minutes to hours, so the calibration is re-measured again and
again. This page treats that drift head-on: as a slowly time-varying system to *identify*, not a
nuisance to average away.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The plant and the scope
This runs on the **new coupled DARM plant** — the M0-damped reduced-QUAD hierarchical actuation
(M0 / PUM / ESD) with coupled detuned-cavity sensing, where the SRC detuning splits the cavity pole
into a complex pair (the same twin as [example 08](08-darm-calibration.qmd)). We build up in three steps: a single
actuation strength κ(t) on a smooth curve, then the SRC detuning δ(t), then the realistic case —
**several parameters drifting at once, at random**, recovered jointly. Still deferred: a
Gaussian-process wander with a measured drift spectrum, all seven TDCFs together, and the one-shot
(rather than two-step) Lataire–Pintelon fit. Rendered with `freeze: true`.
:::

## The idea: locally stationary snapshots

The plant drifts far more slowly than one measurement record (an hour-scale drift versus a
~16 s record), so within any single record it is **locally stationary** — the Pintelon–Schoukens
picture of a linear model around a slowly-moving operating point. That licenses a two-step
estimator:

1. **Snapshot.** At a sequence of times, take one leakage-free periodic-multisine measurement and
   recover the instantaneous actuation strength with **Pcal as the ruler**. Because the sensing
   `C` cancels in the stage-to-Pcal ratio, each snapshot is *immune to sensing drift* and carries
   an honest per-estimate σ.
2. **Basis fit.** Fit `κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a time-basis (Legendre) to the snapshot series by
   weighted least squares — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion in two-step form. The coefficient
   covariance **is** the Cramér–Rao bound on the drift curve κ(t) and its rate.

We drift the **ESD (TST) stage** — the one whose strength really wanders in an interferometer, as
charge builds on the reaction mass — with a 5 %, hour-scale profile, on the coupled reduced-quad
plant (the ruler `H_stage/H_pcal = κ_i·D_i·N_i` recovers κ through the M0-damped compliance and the
nested-offload distribution).

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Run the campaign — snapshot the drift, fit κ(t)"
c = dd.campaign(seed=777)
```

## Tracking the drift

The injected truth, the per-record snapshots with their error bars, and the recovered κ(t) with
its CRB band:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "κ(t): injected truth, snapshots ± σ, LP fit ± CRB"
dd.drift_fig(c)
```

The fit rides straight through the snapshots and follows the injected drift — a 5 % excursion
resolved cleanly, even though each single snapshot only pins κ to about a percent.

## Is the recovery honest?

A curve through points is easy; a curve that knows its own uncertainty is the point. The recovery
residual (recovered − truth) stays inside the ±σ Cramér–Rao band — the error bar neither
collapses (which would be fabricated confidence) nor balloons (which would be uselessly
conservative):

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Tracking error vs the CRB band"
dd.tracking_error_fig(c)
```

## The feasibility gate: is the drift resolvable?

Before calling a drift "trackable" or "buried in noise," compute the bound. The tracking σ from the
fit is far below the injected drift amplitude, so the drift is genuinely **resolved**, not noise —
and the local-stationarity approximation costs a fraction of a percent, well under the per-snapshot
error:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Resolvability — a computed bound, not an eyeball"
display(dd.resolvability_table(c))
```

The resolve ratio is a knob, not a limit: more periods per snapshot, more snapshots, or a stronger
drive all buy it down further — the same Fisher levers as everywhere else in the pipeline.

## The new physics: a drifting SRC detuning δ(t)

The coupled plant lets us track the drift that the old single-pole twin could not represent: the
**SRC detuning δ**. As the SRC error point wanders around its slightly-detuned operating point, the
cavity pole moves — splitting toward a complex pair — and the sensing shape changes with it. δ is a
*sensing* parameter, so it does **not** cancel in the κ ruler; instead it is recovered from the
**Pcal FRF shape** (`C_meas = H_pcal·(1+G)`), which makes the δ snapshot independent of the κ drift
— the two compose into a joint κ(t), δ(t) picture. We drift δ by 5 % around a 5° operating point:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Snapshot the drifting SRC detuning δ(t) from the Pcal FRF, fit δ(t)"
cd = dd.campaign_delta(seed=778)
dd.delta_drift_fig(cd)
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "δ(t) resolvability — a computed bound"
display(dd.delta_resolvability_table(cd))
```

The detuning is recovered to a hundredth of a degree per snapshot — the coupled-cavity split leaves
a strong high-frequency signature in `C`, so δ is well-identified even at this small detuning. Note
the separation of concerns: κ comes from the stage/Pcal *ratio* (immune to sensing drift), δ from
the Pcal *shape* (immune to actuation drift), so a real interferometer's simultaneous κ- and
δ-drift are tracked by two independent snapshots on the same records.

## Round 2: everything drifts at once, and at random

The two sections above each drift **one** parameter along a **smooth** curve. Reality is messier on
both counts: several calibration numbers wander **simultaneously**, and the wander is **random**
(a meandering walk), not a tidy sine. Here we do both — the optical gain `κ_C`, the SRC detuning
`δ`, and the ESD strength `κ_ESD` all drift together as random (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck) walks, and each
record is fit for **all three at once**. A joint fit is essential because the parameters are not
independent: a wobble in one can masquerade as a wobble in another, and only a joint fit — with the
Pcal record pinning the sensing and each stage record pinning its own strength — untangles them.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Three random drifts at once, recovered in one joint fit per record"
cj = dd.campaign_joint(seed=2024)
dd.joint_drift_fig(cj)
```

All three random wanders are followed within their error bars. The **correlation matrix** of a
single snapshot shows *how well* they separate:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Which drifts are hard to tell apart"
dd.joint_corr_fig(cj)
```

`δ` separates cleanly from the two gains (near-zero correlation) — it lives in the sensing *shape*,
which the amplitudes don't touch. But `κ_C` (optical gain) and `κ_ESD` (test-mass drive) are
strongly **anti-correlated**: both simply scale the ESD line, so the loop shape alone cannot tell an
optical-gain change from an actuation change — it is the **Pcal absolute reference** that breaks the
tie (exactly why Pcal is the fiducial in a real calibration). The joint fit surfaces that degeneracy
honestly rather than hiding it in a one-at-a-time recovery.

## Designing the drive: a few optimal lines, not broadband

The rounds above inject a **broadband** multisine — power in every bin — which is *not* how a real
calibration drives the interferometer, and *not* what optimal excitation calls for. The plant is
**one** system (the opto-mechanical DARM sensing `C` plus the quad suspension) with **one** joint
parameter vector, and it is read out by a **few always-on calibration lines**. The right question
is where to *put* those lines. Given a prior on how much each parameter drifts, we place and weight
a handful of lines — Pcal lines plus one per in-band stage — to **minimise the joint estimator
variance on the drifts** (a Bayesian A-optimal design), under the **real force budgets**: the Pcal's
±200 mW photon-calibrator range, and each suspension stage capped at the same displacement ruler.

Every line informs every parameter — a suspension line passes through `C` and `1/(1+G)` so it
carries sensing information, and the Pcal ruler, compared against a suspension line, carries
actuation information — so the design works on the **coupled** Fisher matrix, not two separate
problems.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Design the A-optimal cal-line roster and score it against a broadband drive"
dc = dd.design_campaign()
dd.design_fig(dc)
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Per-parameter drift prior, snapshot σ, and the resolvability margin"
display(dd.design_table(dc))
```

A **handful** of designed lines reaches a lower joint cost than a broadband multisine that spends the
same budget over ~six times as many lines — the drive belongs where each parameter is informative,
not spread thin across the band (much of which is the seismic wall or a stage's dead zone). Injecting
exactly this roster on the twin and reading it back leakage-free recovers the drifting parameters:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Track the joint set from the DESIGNED cal-line readout (not broadband)"
tc = dd.tracked_lines_campaign()
dd.tracked_lines_fig(tc)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What's grounded, and what the scope is
The **κ_C drift prior is measured** (Sun et al. 2020: the optical gain varies 1–2 % over a run); the
**Pcal budget is real** (±200 mW → `pcal_range_disp`); the **O4 line frequencies are published**
(Wade et al. 2025, Fig. 4). The drift priors for `δ`, `κ_PUM`, `κ_ESD` are **representative
placeholders** — the O3/O4 papers do not quantify them — and the per-stage force caps are **derived**
by matching the Pcal ruler, since the papers give no per-stage line amplitude. The design tracks the
**identifiable joint set** for this twin and the O4 floor: `κ_C`, `δ`, and the two in-band stages
`κ_PUM`/`κ_ESD`. The other TDCFs are feasibility-gated, not hidden:

- **`κ_M0`** — the design frequency band runs down to **1 Hz** (there is no arbitrary cap), and the
  placement uses the honest **seismic wall** extrapolated below 10 Hz (`darm_o4_asd_seismic`, ≈ f⁻⁷).
  With that real floor the top mass is squeezed out from both sides: below ~10 Hz the seismic wall
  buries its line, and above ~10 Hz its own hierarchical offload rolls its DARM authority off as
  ≈ f⁻⁸. A leakage-free simulation confirms the line cannot be recovered anywhere in band, so
  `κ_M0` is **not** claimed here — it would need a sub-Hz line, where the detector is deaf. (The
  analytic Fisher is optimistic for this offloaded stage; the simulation is the arbiter.)
- **`f_cc`/`τ`** need a wideband high-frequency Pcal spread to become well-conditioned.

The joint Fisher (`darm_callines.joint_fisher`) plus the simulated readout together say what each of
those would require, rather than reporting a number the simulation won't back up.
:::

## Honest gaps

On the coupled reduced-quad plant, the machinery now tracks **several parameters drifting at once,
under a realistic random wander, within a Cramér–Rao bound, from a P&S-optimal designed cal-line
drive** — and the correlation matrix names the degeneracies instead of hiding them. What's still
simplified: the random walk is a plain Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (a Gaussian-process wander with a
measured drift spectrum is the honest next step); the estimator is the two-step form (snapshot, then
basis-fit) rather than the one-shot Lataire–Pintelon fit; the drift priors for all but `κ_C` are
representative placeholders pending real per-parameter numbers; and `κ_M0`, `f_cc`, `τ` need the
out-of-band / wideband lines noted above to join the tracked set. What this page establishes is the
foundation: the "can we track it?" question gets a numeric answer, jointly, from an optimal drive,
and honestly — see `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`.
